Western EuropeHeat wave · May 22–31, 2026

### See the heat build across Europe

**7.25days**

Sustained agreement with the regional peak temperature

WeatherMesh settled within 1°C of the May 26 regional temperature peak more than a week ahead, and stayed there in every later forecast—12 hours before AIFS.

Across the UK study region, Germany, France and Spain, WeatherMesh had lower temperature error than IFS at six reported leads from one to fifteen days.

Key takeaways

- A sustained signal for the regional peak from the May 19, 12 UTC forecast.
- Lower error than IFS across the reported 1–15 day leads; AIFS led at six days.

Study details & evidence+

#### About this study

The heat wave's peak is taken as the combined study region's temperature at 18 UTC on May 26 (26.6°C in ERA5). From the May 19, 12 UTC run onward, about a week before the peak, every WeatherMesh forecast stayed within 1°C of it. AIFS reached that accuracy 12 hours later. IFS and GFS did not reach it in any of the runs tested.

Temperature errors cover forecasts valid at 12 UTC on May 22–31. Only initialization and valid-time pairs available for every model are used. Land points are sampled on a common 0.5° grid and weighted by latitude. The UK region also includes Ireland and a small part of northern France.

WeatherMesh, IFS and AIFS are ensemble means; GFS is a single deterministic run. The accompanying map is a separate seven-day forecast, issued May 19 at 12 UTC and valid May 26 at 12 UTC, six hours before the headline peak.

This is a single heat wave, with 7–10 matched valid times per lead time. AIFS was the stronger model at many medium-range lead times in the UK and Germany. ERA5 is a reanalysis used as the reference, not direct station observations. The midday and early-evening samples are not daily maximum temperatures.

TexasFern · Jan 24–29, 2026

### A clearer view of the Texas freeze

**50%**

Lower temperature error than IFS at 5–7 days

WeatherMesh averaged 2.37°C of temperature error versus 4.78°C for ECMWF’s IFS ensemble, verified against observations at 10 Texas airports.

The length of the freeze mattered, too. Around three days before the event, WeatherMesh forecast 51 freezing hours in San Antonio versus IFS’s 19. Observations recorded 69 hours.

Key takeaways

- Lower temperature error than IFS, AIFS and GFS in both the 5–7 and 7–10 day bands.
- A closer estimate of San Antonio’s prolonged freeze, relevant to planning for sustained heating demand.

Study details & evidence+

#### About this study

Temperature accuracy is measured at 10 Texas airports over January 24–26, against quality-controlled METAR observations. All models are compared on the same forecast runs, valid times and stations.

The long-lead WeatherMesh results come from a retrospective backtest of the ensemble mean. A separate freeze-duration analysis covers January 24–29, with lead times measured to the start of that window.

The maps show seven-day forecasts issued January 18 and valid January 25 at 00 UTC, compared against ERA5 reanalysis. ERA5 is used only for the maps. The temperature-error chart is scored against station observations.

This is a single, selected event. WeatherNext-2 locked onto the peak cold earlier and held it, and it led on freeze duration at leads of 1.5–5 days. At 10–15 days, AIFS had slightly lower temperature error, and all models were too warm.

North AtlanticMelissa · Oct–Nov 2025

### A more accurate track, four days ahead

WeatherMesh **82km**

NHC Official **395km**

Mean track error four days ahead

North of Bermuda, WeatherMesh averaged 79% less track error than NHC Official across five matched four-day forecasts.

A separate retrospective study near Jamaica revealed another benefit: some ensemble members showed a deep low 15 days ahead, while the averaged forecast showed little signal.

Key takeaways

- Track: a closer view of Melissa’s path as it moved into the North Atlantic.
- Ensemble: see stronger-storm possibilities that an averaged forecast can hide.

Study details & evidence+

#### About this study

At a four-day lead, WeatherMesh's mean track error was 82 km, compared with 395 km for the NHC official forecast. Both are verified against five HURDAT2 best-track positions north of Bermuda on October 31–November 1. Individual forecast cycles can be explored on the map.

The ensemble analysis looks at October 28, when Melissa was near Jamaica, using all 128 members from forecasts issued 1 to 15 days ahead. The chart compares the regional minimum pressure in each member, in the ensemble-mean field and in the ERA5 analysis.

The track and ensemble analyses cover different phases of the storm. At 0.25° resolution, the pressure comparison cannot resolve Category 5 intensity and does not show better intensity accuracy than other models. Spread across members is not a calibrated probability for the storm.
